replying_to: Replying to Scalable Option Learning in High-Throughput Environments
display_title: Official Review of Submission12651 by Reviewer 6484

summary.value: This paper proposes Scalable Option Learning (SOL) as a way to scale up Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning to magnitudes more samples. In particular, the paper identifies many scaling challenges related to Hierarchical RL, and proposes valid solutions to these problems to achieve impressive throughput. These include using just a single network for all policies and computing discounted returns for all policies in parallel.

strengths.value:
- The paper is effective in its key goal of improving throughput, which has repeatedly shown to be of great value to the RL community.

- Section 5 does a good job of ablating the contributions of the method, specifically demonstrating where the benefits of the method come from.

- Source code release and key parts of the code already being included make the contribution far more valuable as it can be easily used and adapted.

weaknesses.value:
My primary concern of this paper is the similarity to the existing method, Agent57 [1]. This method also: 
- Learns multiple policies with different tasks (different amounts of intrinsic reward, discount rates, and probability of random actions), all parameterized by a single network.
- Uses a controller to select which policy to execute
- The single network appends a vector indicating which policy is being executed.
- Can achieve massive throughput (Agent57 reaches ~66,560 frames per second on Atari environments, almost 6 years ago, albeit on different hardware).
Additionally, Agent57 also provides in own intrinsic rewards [2] rather than relying on given rewards. While Agent57 does not use hierarchical RL (its controller selects policies for entire episodes), I think the amount of similarity without any acknowledgment or even a citation is problematic.

While acknowledged by the authors, the heavy reliance on a provided intrinsic reward is still problematic. In particular, many such methods are themselves computationally taxing, meaning the effectiveness of this method without provided intrinsic rewards may be greatly reduced.

While performance graphs currently show uncertainty using two standard errors, I’d prefer to see the use of RLiable’s [3] methods. They proposed using 95% confidence intervals when reporting results, and have been considered the highest standard for reporting results for some time.

questions.value:
- I think a diagram of the agent’s network architecture would improve the paper, especially since it is one of the main ways higher throughput is achieved. Would it be possible to provide this in an appendix?

- As mentioned, this method has numerous similarities to Agent57. I would appreciate a detailed comparison of these methods, and exactly what the novelty of your method is in comparison. I would be very interested to see the performance of SOL on the Atari benchmark for direct comparison, although I understand this may not be possible within the given period.

- Given some existing intrinsic reward methods (such as E3B [4] or any reasonable method you wish), what would the throughput of SOL be, and what would the performance be like compared to the handcrafted rewards?

I do believe this paper would be valuable to the RL community if accepted. If you are able to answer all of my questions sufficiently, I will raise my score. If you can do this and show that your method is competitive with existing work on the Atari benchmark and include these results in the final paper, I will raise my score considerably higher.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission12651 by Reviewer 6484

comment.value:
Thank you for taking the time to review our paper. We are happy that you think the paper would be valuable to the RL community if accepted, and that you appreciated our inclusion of ablations and code details to help reproducibility. We have updated the paper in response to your comments and those of the other reviewers. Please see our answers to your comments below.

> My primary concern of this paper is the similarity to the existing method, Agent57 [1]. [...] As mentioned, this method has numerous similarities to Agent57. I would appreciate a detailed comparison of these methods, and exactly what the novelty of your method is in comparison. 

Thank you for pointing this out. We have added a paragraph in the Related Work discussing the relationship with Agent57, together with a more detailed discussion in Appendix G.1. The key similarities and differences as we see them are:
- Both methods have multiple policies sharing the same neural network, which are indexed by a one-hot vector. This allows both of them to achieve high throughput by batching forward passes. 
- A key difference is that SOL switches between different sub-policies within the same episode, whereas Agent57 executes the same sub-policy for the entire episode. Switching between different sub-policies is essential for the tasks we consider, i.e. alternating between fighting and healing in NetHack (we illustrate this in Appendix F.2).

The above difference influences several of the systems-level designs we describe in Section 3.3. For example:
- The fact that the controller is observation-conditioned requires a different neural network architecture that also outputs distributions over options and option execution lengths, in addition to low-level environment actions. We have added a figure to clarify this in Appendix E.2.  
- It also requires our environment wrapper in the actor workers to duplicate observations each time the controller is called and record the currently active option and option execution length. 
- Switching between different option policies within the same episode also requires particular handling of the return/advantage computations. Each time the option policy changes (say from option A to option B), we need to bootstrap the returns of option A using the last observation where option A was active and mask the future rewards gathered when executing option B. 

We have added a discussion of all these points in Appendix G.1, which we refer to in the section on Agent57 we have added in Related Work. 

> While acknowledged by the authors, the heavy reliance on a provided intrinsic reward is still problematic. In particular, many such methods are themselves computationally taxing, meaning the effectiveness of this method without provided intrinsic rewards may be greatly reduced.

We agree that assuming option rewards are available is a limitation. However, we believe the question of how to automatically learn good option rewards is orthogonal to the question of how to scale hierarchical learning, which is the primary focus of this work. We are currently investigating combining SOL with intrinsic rewards and will let you know if we have results by the end of the rebuttal period. Based on our preliminary experiments, RND does not significantly slow down either our base flat RL algorithm or SOL, since it only requires one additional pass through the predictor and target networks to compute the intrinsic rewards. Therefore we do not see this as being a fundamental limitation. 


> While performance graphs currently show uncertainty using two standard errors, I’d prefer to see the use of RLiable’s [3] methods. They proposed using 95% confidence intervals when reporting results, and have been considered the highest standard for reporting results for some time.

We agree that RLiable is a great tool for computing aggregate metrics together with confidence intervals over benchmarks which include multiple tasks. This is especially useful for benchmarks with many tasks (such as Atari/DeepMind Control/Procgen) for which reporting performance curves for all individual tasks would be hard to understand. However, our empirical evaluation focuses on fewer tasks which are either very rich and complex (NetHack) or specifically targeted to measure the ability to perform hard credit assignment (MiniHack and G-Maze). Therefore, we found that reporting results for each task individually was easy to understand and gave more fine-grained information than aggregate statistics. We note that two standard errors also correspond to a 95% confidence interval around the mean for normally distributed samples, hence we believe the differences we observe between different methods are statistically reliable.

comment.value:
In addition to our above response, we have some new results which we believe further address one of the reviewers’ previous comments. 

> While acknowledged by the authors, the heavy reliance on a provided intrinsic reward is still problematic. In particular, many such methods are themselves computationally taxing, meaning the effectiveness of this method without provided intrinsic rewards may be greatly reduced.

We have updated the paper with additional experiments (Section 5.3) which show that SOL can be combined with option rewards learned automatically using DIAYN [1]. We have evaluated SOL+DIAYN on both MiniHack environments, where it closely matches SOL with handcoded option rewards and significantly outperforms the flat baselines. Furthermore, the drop in throughput from adding DIAYN-based rewards is small (~7%), since this can be done on the GPU in the learner thread. We hope this addresses the reviewer’s concern about our use of handcoded option rewards, by showing that SOL’s innovations are independent of how option rewards are defined, and that it is compatible with both handcoded and learned ones.

[1] “Diversity is All You Need: Learning Skills Without a Reward Function.” Eysenbach et al., ICLR 2019.

replying_to: Replying to Scalable Option Learning in High-Throughput Environments
display_title: Official Review of Submission12651 by Reviewer gHuB

summary.value:
The paper introduces Scalable Option Learning (SOL), a hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm designed to scale online hierarchical RL to high-throughput environments with billions of samples. Building on the options framework, SOL jointly optimizes a controller policy and multiple option policies using actor-critic objectives, assuming access to intrinsic reward functions for each option. It enables ~35-580x higher throughput compared to prior hierarchical methods like HIRO, Option-Critic, and MOC, while retaining 86% of flat PPO's speed.
It is evaluated on challenging environments: NetHack, custom MiniHack tasks, and MuJoCo PointMaze. Results highlight SOL's ability to learn complementary options, adapt option lengths, and scale effectively.

strengths.value:
The paper identifies critical bottlenecks in scaling hierarchical RL (e.g., non-parallelizable forward passes and return computations due to dynamic policy switching) and provides elegant, systems-level solutions.

Experiments are comprehensive and challenging. Training on 30 billion steps in NetHack (a sparse, long-horizon, partially observable environment) is impressive and demonstrates positive scaling trends, surpassing flat PPO and hierarchical baselines like HiPPO.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Lack of Clarity for Broader Audiences:**
The paper assumes familiarity with hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) and high-throughput RL, which may make it challenging for readers less versed in these areas. For instance, it does not clearly delineate scenarios where HRL is advantageous, such as long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards (e.g., NetHack’s dungeon navigation or robotics with delayed feedback) or settings requiring complex behavior coordination (e.g., switching between fighting and healing). Similarly, the relationship between HRL and high-throughput RL is underexplored; while SOL bridges these by enabling parallelized training for HRL, the paper could better explain how HRL’s task decomposition complements high-throughput RL’s scalability to make its contributions more accessible. A brief primer on when and why HRL is needed, and its synergy with large-scale training, would enhance clarity for a wider audience.
2. **Limited Performance Comparisons with Prior HRL Methods:**
While the paper compares SOL’s throughput to prior HRL algorithms (HIRO, Option-Critic, MOC, Hierarchical RLLib), it omits these as performance baselines in key experiments like NetHack and MiniHack, relying instead on flat RL (APPO), SOL-HiPPO, and Motif. This choice is not well-explained, leaving it unclear why established HRL methods are excluded from performance evaluations. The likely reason—computational infeasibility due to their low throughput (55-1,200 steps/second vs. SOL’s 43,000)—is not explicitly stated, nor are challenges like adapting these methods to NetHack’s symbolic inputs. Including MOC only in MuJoCo and not NetHack further muddles the comparison scope. Explicitly addressing these omissions would strengthen the paper’s rigor and clarify SOL’s standing relative to prior HRL work.
3. **Dependence on Predefined Option Rewards:**
SOL’s performance heavily relies on predefined intrinsic rewards for options (e.g., ΔHealth, ΔScore in NetHack), which require domain knowledge to design. Experiments show that without these rewards, SOL-HiPPO (using only task rewards) performs similarly to flat APPO, suggesting that the hierarchical architecture’s benefits are contingent on well-crafted rewards. This raises questions about the architecture’s standalone effectiveness, as the hierarchy alone does not consistently outperform flat RL without intrinsic guidance.

4. **Unclear Scalability Advantage of Dual-Policy Training:**
The paper claims that SOL’s hierarchical approach, involving training both a controller and option policies, is more scalable than traditional single-policy RL, but this is not convincingly justified. Intuitively, training two policies (controller and options) should increase computational complexity compared to a single flat policy (e.g., PPO). While SOL’s innovations—such as a unified neural network, environment wrapper, and parallelized computations—enable high throughput, these appear as engineering optimizations rather than fundamental algorithmic advances.

The reason you state is correct: we were not able to include the other hierarchical baselines because it would take infeasibly long to run them (the fastest, MOC, would take > 1 month for MiniHack, > 9 months on NetHack, the others would take even longer). We did include MOC on Mujoco because it is a simpler environment that requires much less samples for the algorithms to converge. We have added a paragraph in Section 5 of the updated paper to clarify this point. 


> Dependence on Predefined Option Rewards: SOL’s performance heavily relies on predefined intrinsic rewards for options (e.g., ΔHealth, ΔScore in NetHack), which require domain knowledge to design. Experiments show that without these rewards, SOL-HiPPO (using only task rewards) performs similarly to flat APPO, suggesting that the hierarchical architecture’s benefits are contingent on well-crafted rewards. This raises questions about the architecture’s standalone effectiveness, as the hierarchy alone does not consistently outperform flat RL without intrinsic guidance.


We agree that assuming option rewards are available is a limitation. However, we believe the question of how to automatically learn good option rewards is orthogonal to the question of how to scale hierarchical learning, which is the primary focus of this work. We do hope to remove this limitation in future work, and by sharing our code we also make it easier for others to work on it at scale. Also, note that we compare to flat baselines which also have access to the same intrinsic rewards (denoted `APPO (task+options rewards)`), which perform worse. This illustrates that adding prior knowledge in the form of intrinsic rewards is not necessarily sufficient in itself, and hierarchy is needed to unlock its benefits. 


> Unclear Scalability Advantage of Dual-Policy Training: The paper claims that SOL’s hierarchical approach, involving training both a controller and option policies, is more scalable than traditional single-policy RL, but this is not convincingly justified. Intuitively, training two policies (controller and options) should increase computational complexity compared to a single flat policy (e.g., PPO). [...]

We would like to clarify that we do not claim that our hierarchical approach is more scalable than a flat single-policy approach. Rather, our claim is that our method enables hierarchical agents to be trained at a comparable scale as high-throughput flat agents (~86% in our experiments), which was previously not possible for the reasons described in Section 3.2. If there is a particular part of the paper that suggests otherwise, please let us know and we will clarify it. 

We hope our clarifications and paper updates have addressed your concerns, and that you will consider raising your score to recommend acceptance. If you still have concerns which are not addressed, please let us know as soon as possible and we will do our best to address them.

Thanks for your response.

About claims on "flat" vs "hierarchical": In Section 6, "When trained at scale on the challenging NetHack Learning Environment, our algorithm surpasses flat baselines".

I keep my concerns about the assumption limitation and that SOL’s innovations appear as engineering optimizations rather than fundamental algorithmic advances (also mentioned by other reviewers).

display_title: Official Review of Submission12651 by Reviewer gDaQ

summary.value: The paper introduces Scalable Option Learning (SOL), a hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm that scales to billions of samples in high-throughput environments. Its main contribution is overcoming the system-level bottlenecks that have so far limited the scalability of hierarchical RL compared to flat agents.

strengths.value: The paper is well written and clearly structured, making it easy to follow. The proposed solution is presented in a clear way, and the experimental results appear solid and convincing.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper’s novelty lies primarily in systems-level design. While the throughput improvements are impressive, the core RL algorithmic advances are modest, with most contributions being engineering optimizations rather than new principles for hierarchical learning.

2. The evaluation focuses mainly on NetHack and MiniHack, with only a simple PointMaze task in MuJoCo. Although the proposed solutions are promising and could have broader impact, this potential is not fully demonstrated within the current set of experiments.

3. The framework assumes access to well-defined intrinsic option rewards, which is a strong assumption. In their absence, hierarchical RL provides no clear advantage over flat RL, highlighting a key limitation of the approach.

questions.value:
1. In Section 3.3, paragraph Architecture, the one-hot vector $u$ is introduced to determine whether an option policy or the controller policy is active. How is $u$ updated during training and execution? Is it managed solely by the environment wrapper, or is there any learning signal associated with it?

2. IMPALA's V-trace employs an off-policy correction term to account for lag between the actors and the learner in asynchronous settings. In your method, the value objective $V^{\omega}(s_t)$ does not appear to include such a correction . Could you clarify why this choice was made? In practice, is there a noticeable lag between the actor policies and the learner’s most recent version, and if so, how is this handled?

comment.value:
Thank you for taking the time to review our paper, and we are glad you found our experimental results solid and convincing. We have updated the paper in response to your comments and those of the other reviewers. Please see our answers to your specific comments below.

> The paper’s novelty lies primarily in systems-level design. While the throughput improvements are impressive, the core RL algorithmic advances are modest, with most contributions being engineering optimizations rather than new principles for hierarchical learning.

We agree that scaling is the primary focus, and believe that this is a valid contribution given that many recent advances in AI have been achieved through scaling. To our knowledge, the ideas presented here which enable this kind of scaling are novel. Also, note that the hierarchical design helps unlock the benefits of scale: we also compare to flat policies scaled with the same amount of data/compute, but this does not translate into higher performance.

> The evaluation focuses mainly on NetHack and MiniHack, with only a simple PointMaze task in MuJoCo. Although the proposed solutions are promising and could have broader impact, this potential is not fully demonstrated within the current set of experiments.

One of the main reasons for this is that many standard RL benchmarks (Mujoco, DMC, Atari) are relatively short horizon and/or are solvable by flat policies - we hope more benchmarks become available in the future, since this is an important problem. 


> The framework assumes access to well-defined intrinsic option rewards, which is a strong assumption. In their absence, hierarchical RL provides no clear advantage over flat RL, highlighting a key limitation of the approach.

We recognize this is a limitation. However, we believe that the question of how to automatically learn good option rewards is orthogonal to the question of how to scale hierarchical learning, which is the primary focus of this work. We hope to address this in future work, and by sharing our code we also make it easier for others to work on it at scale. 

> In Section 3.3, paragraph Architecture, the one-hot vector u is introduced to determine whether an option policy or the controller policy is active. How is u updated during training and execution? Is it managed solely by the environment wrapper, or is there any learning signal associated with it?

The $u$ vector is governed by the controller, which outputs two quantities at each call: which option to execute next (call it $\omega$), and how many steps to execute it for (call it $l$). Both of these are recorded in the environment wrapper. The vector $u$ is then set to $\omega$ for the next $l$ steps, after which it reverts back to the controller. The controller is then called again, which resets $u$ to one of the option policies for some number of steps, and the process continues. The $u$ vector is included in the observation returned by the environment wrapper, which is then fed to the network. We have updated the “Actor Worker” paragraph to make this clearer. 

> IMPALA's V-trace employs an off-policy correction term to account for lag between the actors and the learner in asynchronous settings. In your method, the value objective  does not appear to include such a correction . Could you clarify why this choice was made? In practice, is there a noticeable lag between the actor policies and the learner’s most recent version, and if so, how is this handled?

We do in fact use this off-policy correction, in SOL’s V-trace code in Appendix E.3 there is a `ratio` field which represents the ratio between the probabilities of the policy used to collect the data and the current policy. We did not include this in the equations of Section 3.1 to keep the notation light and have equations fit on one line. We have added a sentence clarifying this point in the “Learner Worker” paragraph of Section 3.3 in the updated paper. Thank you for pointing this out. 

We hope that our clarifications and paper updates have addressed your comments, and that you would consider raising your score to a solid accept. If you have remaining concerns that prevent you from doing so, please let us know and we will do our best to address them.
I want to thank the authors for their responses. I do not have any follow-up questions and I am satisfied with their answers. I will update my score accordingly.

display_title: Official Review of Submission12651 by Reviewer sjdv

summary.value: The paper proposes Scalable Option Learning, a hierarchical RL framework optimized for high-throughput distributed training. The method unifies multiple option policies into a single network with masking and parallel advantage computation, enabling efficient batching on GPUs. Experiments on the NetHack Learning Environment and MiniHack claim large throughput gains (35–580x) over prior hierarchical baselines and improved learning performance in long-horizon tasks.

strengths.value:
- Well-executed system engineering that integrates hierarchy into scalable RL pipelines.
- Strong empirical demonstration on NetHack.
- Transparent reporting of hyperparameters and ablations.
- The throughput improvements are impressive, even if largely due to implementation efficiency.

weaknesses.value:
- The paper mentions option-specific reward signals but does not describe a general way to derive them. If these require manual tuning, applicability beyond benchmark tasks is uncertain.
- The learning formulation largely reuses option-critic ideas, the primary novelty lies in batching and software efficiency.
- The main empirical evidence comes from NetHack. Additional results on diverse continuous-control or multi-task domains would strengthen generality claims.
- The paper includes descriptive visualizations of option usage but no quantitative diversity metrics (mutual information, entropy). It remains unclear whether options represent meaningful temporal abstractions or redundant sub-policies.
- Gains may partly reflect different batching or hardware configurations, compute-normalized comparisons would be more informative.

questions.value:
- How are the intrinsic rewards defined in each environment? Are they fixed heuristics or learned?
- How sensitive is SOL’s performance to these reward definitions or scaling factors?
- Are gradient interferences between option heads and the shared trunk observed, and if so, how are they mitigated?
- Can the same design support multi-level hierarchies (options over options)?
- How is throughput measured and normalized (environment frames per second, learner updates per wall-clock second, ...)?

comment.value:
Thank you for taking the time to review our paper. We have updated the paper in response to your comments and those of the other reviewers. Please see our answers to your specific comments below. 



> The paper mentions option-specific reward signals but does not describe a general way to derive them. If these require manual tuning, applicability beyond benchmark tasks is uncertain. [...]
> How are the intrinsic rewards defined in each environment? Are they fixed heuristics or learned?

The option rewards are fixed heuristics here. For all the tasks we consider, these are very simple to define or are even provided by default as part of standard codebases or gym environments. Ideally we would like to remove this assumption, but believe the question of how to automatically learn good option rewards is orthogonal to the question of how to scale hierarchical learning, which is the primary focus of this work. We hope to address this in future work, and by sharing our code we also make it easier for others to work on it at scale. 

> Gains may partly reflect different batching or hardware configurations, compute-normalized comparisons would be more informative.

For our throughput experiments, all methods were run on the same hardware. We also tuned the batch size/number of parallel environments for different methods and reported the configuration with the highest throughput. We have added a mention of this in the main text with a reference to Appendix C.3, where it is described in more detail. 

> The paper includes descriptive visualizations of option usage but no quantitative diversity metrics (mutual information, entropy). It remains unclear whether options represent meaningful temporal abstractions or redundant sub-policies.

In Appendix F.2 (Figure 8), for each option we plot the average returns according to different metrics (change in score, change in health). These metrics differ significantly between options, which indicates that the options induce different behaviors at the trajectory level. In addition, as suggested by the reviewer, we have added an information-theoretic measure of redundancy (normalized mutual information) between action distributions of different option policies, shown in Table 8 of Appendix F.2. This gives a more fine-grained measure of redundancy and further confirms that the option policies are not very redundant. 

>How sensitive is SOL’s performance to these reward definitions or scaling factors?

We agree this is an important factor, when considering the generality of our method without needing excessive hyperparameter tuning. We have added an additional ablation experiment measuring the effect of changing the reward scaling factors on both MiniHack environments (Appendix F.4, Figure 13). Overall the performance is quite robust, with a fairly wide range of values around the defaults for which we get similar results. We have added a reference to this experiment in the main text. 

We also have experiments in Appendix F.4 measuring how performance changes on the MiniHack environments when irrelevant option rewards are added. This slows down learning (which is expected, since the agent cannot know beforehand that a given option is unhelpful and must learn this through experience), but the agent eventually converges to the same performance as an agent who only has useful option rewards. This provides evidence that SOL has some degree of robustness to irrelevant rewards. 


> Are gradient interferences between option heads and the shared trunk observed, and if so, how are they mitigated?

There is actually a single action head for all options (with a separate action head for the controller, since its action space is different), and a single value head - the different options and the controller are indexed by a one-hot vector fed as input to the network. We have added a figure in Appendix E.2. showing the neural network architecture in detail to make this clearer, and added a reference in the Architecture paragraph of Section 3.3.

> Can the same design support multi-level hierarchies (options over options)?

In principle yes, with a few modifications to our environment wrapper. A nice feature of our method is that both our modified network architecture and parallelized V-trace do not distinguish between different policies in the hierarchy: the controller and option policies are all handled the same way (they are indexed by a one-hot vector input to the network, and their returns are computed in parallel the same way). We think this is exciting future work, and by open sourcing our code we hope to make it easy for the community to explore this and other extensions.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission12651 by Area Chair MVim

summary.value:
The paper focuses on scalable option learning, which is a hierarchical RL approach that achieves a higher throughput than existing methods. The authors validate the empirical strength of their technique on MiniHack and Mujoco environments.

While three reviewers had favorable opinions on the paper, reviewer gHuB remained critical, stating that the merits "appear as engineering optimizations rather than fundamental algorithmic advances (also mentioned by other reviewers)".

I believe the methodological novelty of the method needs to be better motivated, and the performance needs to be clearly delineated from existing approaches. The authors should differentiate the engineering optimizations from the algorithmic advances in a clearer manner.

As a result, I propose rejecting the paper in its current form.

reviewer_concerns.value: The concerns of reviewer gHuB are not addressed.

reviewer_scores.value: Reviewer gHuB mentioned that they will keep their current score, while reviewer gDaQ would update their score.
